name: Asa
bio:
Asa was Abijam's son, who succeeded him as king of Judah and reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem (1 Kings 15:8-10). Chronicles records that the land was at peace for the first ten years of his reign, during which Asa removed pagan altars and high places, commanded Judah to seek the LORD, and built fortified cities while there was no war. With an army of 300,000 from Judah and 280,000 from Benjamin, he then faced an enormous invading force under Zerah the Cushite, a million strong with 300 chariots, at Mareshah. Asa cried out, "LORD, there is no one like you to help the powerless against the mighty... we rely on you, and in your name we have come against this vast army," and the LORD struck down the Cushites before him; Asa's army pursued them all the way to Gerar, plundering the surrounding towns and herds before returning to Jerusalem with great spoil (2 Chronicles 14:1-15). Afterward, the prophet Azariah son of Oded met Asa and declared that the LORD would stay with him only as long as he sought the LORD, warning that Israel had once suffered great turmoil for going without the true God and a teaching priest. Encouraged, Asa removed detestable idols from Judah, Benjamin, and the cities he had taken in the hill country of Ephraim, and restored the altar of the LORD. He gathered Judah, Benjamin, and many who had defected from the northern tribes at Jerusalem, where they sacrificed from the plunder of Zerah's army and entered a solemn covenant, under penalty of death, to seek the LORD wholeheartedly; all Judah rejoiced, and the LORD gave them rest (2 Chronicles 15:1-15). Unlike his father and grandfather, Asa did what was right in the LORD's eyes, as David had: he expelled the shrine prostitutes from the land, removed the idols his predecessors had made, and even deposed his own grandmother Maachah from her position as queen mother because she had made a detestable Asherah pole, which Asa cut down and burned in the Kidron Valley. Though the high places were not removed, "Asa's heart was fully committed to the LORD all his life," and he brought the silver, gold, and articles he and his father had dedicated into the temple (1 Kings 15:11-15).

There was war between Asa and Baasha, king of Israel, throughout their reigns. When Baasha fortified Ramah to blockade Judah, cutting off all movement to and from Jerusalem, Asa emptied the treasuries of the temple and palace and sent the silver and gold to Ben-Hadad, king of Aram in Damascus, to persuade him to break his treaty with Baasha and attack Israel instead. Ben-Hadad agreed, attacking several of Israel's northern cities, which forced Baasha to abandon his fortification of Ramah; Asa then had all Judah carry away the stone and timber Baasha had used and used it to fortify Geba and Mizpah instead (1 Kings 15:16-22). Chronicles records that Hanani the seer confronted Asa over this very alliance, rebuking him for relying on the king of Aram instead of the LORD who had once delivered Zerah's huge army into his hand, and warning that wars would follow for this folly; Asa, enraged, threw Hanani in prison and oppressed some of his own people at the same time (2 Chronicles 16:1-10). Asa suffered from a disease in his feet in his old age, and even then sought help only from physicians rather than the LORD (2 Chronicles 16:12). When he died in the forty-first year of his reign, he was buried with his ancestors in a tomb he had cut for himself in the City of David, laid on a bier with spices and perfumes prepared by skilled craftsmen amid a great funeral fire in his honor, and his son Jehoshaphat succeeded him (1 Kings 15:23-24; 2 Chronicles 16:13-14).
